utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- able to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought in, I just wanted to put something on the record with respect to the documents that were brought by the witness on Friday and taken possession of by the OTP. I just wand to update the Court and I believe Defence counsel already know this but just in case, to make it absolutely clear. Over the weekend, the Prosecution was able to analyse those documents and translate certain ones of them. Some of the documents are already in evidence and just so the record is clear I'll set out which ones are already in evidence: A document which is in P49, P049 at U008-1621 was provided by the witness. A document which is in evidence in P48 at U003-8613 and 8614 is already in evidence. And just to be clear, the witness provided an Albanian version of that. What we have in evidence is the English version, but it's the same political declaration, number 12. A document which appears in P049 at U008-1630. And then finally a document which was admitted into evidence on Friday as P139. It's U008-6944 and 6945. Now, there are three documents which were provided by the witness which are not in evidence and those three documents have been translated and provided to the Defence and to the Court, and I will address those with the witness. And just so the record is clear, they are a speech dated 3, 4 March, and the year is written on the document as 1989, though I suspect that's an error and it's 1998. But we'll clarify that with the witness. A document dated 29 April, 1998, and a document dated 28 July 1998. As I said, I'll address those with the witness. With that clarification, I think the witness can be brought in to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have the witness then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi. If I could remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence; it still applies. Mr. Whiting will now continue with his questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Are you able to hear me clearly? You're getting the translation okay?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes. I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Over the weekend we were able to review the documents which you provided on Friday. I can inform you that some of the documents that you provided are already in the possession of the Court -- are in fact already in evidence. But there were three documents that we did not have until you provided them for us, and I'd like to put those documents before you one at a time and ask you some questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher if we could put the first one, which is the document which is dated 3, 4 March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in -- it's handwritten at the top of the document. There's a date which appears to be 3, 4 March, 1989. Is that year correct or is there an error in the year?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an error. It's 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what this is, please.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document represents a statement, a speech, that I held on the occasion of the funeral of the victims who were massacred by the Serbian police. It was held in the municipality of Drenoc, Skenderaj during March 1998, 28th February, 1998 and 1 March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to some paragraphs that are about halfway through the document. I think it's the -- I believe it's the second paragraph on page 2 of the Albanian version. In the English version it's halfway down on the second page. And I'll read out the two paragraphs. "We also warn all the international mechanisms -- the UN, the SC, the USA, the EU, the EP, etc. -- to respect the Charters and documents, which they have themselves drafted and signed, from the Atlantic one to that of Helsinki and Paris. "We are fully confident that in none of the mentioned valid documents can the defending of one's national threshold and dignity be assessed as a terrorist act. Not a single liberation war in any country of the world has been qualified as a terrorist one, and our war is nothing but a liberation one. If we chose to exercise terrorism we would surely do it in Serbia and not in our homes. Serbia has a lot of purely Serbian towns." And then I think it's written in handwriting. "Can a woman within the boundaries of her own house be called a terrorist?" Now, was that part of the speech that you gave?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on the -- what's addressed there with respect to defending the movement of the KLA as not being a terrorist movement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Honourable Judges, this was a speech that I held at the time when I was a leader of the LDK in Drenoc. The speech was held on behalf of the two municipalities of Drenica, Skenderaj and Drenoc [as interpreted] and in the name of all political bodies that at the time were active in Drenoc and Skenderaj. The massacre was mainly aimed at civilian population, unarmed population, and only because after the armed crash between the KLA and police -- Serbian police in which the Serb forces were defeated. And the then-regime sent to Drenoc in the villages of Qirez and Likoshan a combat machinery consisting of policemen, paramilitaries, who were all under one command which was the command to exercise terror and genocide over the civilian population. On this day, meaning on the day this speech was held, I don't remember exactly but I think it was 3rd or 4th of March, 1998, on the occasion of the funeral of 40 victims, 11 of which were civilians, people who were taken from their homes. This funeral was attended by over 200.000 citizens from all over Kosova and from abroad. In this time we asked from the international community to impose to Serbia, to impose the then-Belgrade regime to respect the international conventions, not to use and exercise terror and violence over the unarmed population. And of course, to ask from Serbia and its supporters who at the time called the KLA terrorists -- the KLA even in other documents by the Prosecution is viewed as a criminal enterprise. I would here stress again that the KLA was supported by all the population in Kosovo and by the diaspora in the western Europe and in the United States, all over the world, wherever there were Albanians. So how can it be to call an organisation a terrorist enterprise when such an organisation enjoyed the support of all its people and international support as well? And thanks to this support, the Albanian population, the Albanian people in Kosova, now live without that violence that at that time was exercised by that Serb police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd ask that this be given a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P141.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the usher I'd like to put before you, sir, another document which you provided to us on Friday. It's a communique which is dated 29 April, 1998, and appears to be published in Bujku. And if you could just take a moment to look at that. Was this communique issued by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it is a Political Statement Number 2 of the Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. I want to draw your attention to point number 3 where it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this also appears on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where it reads: "The KLA condemns terrorism and other forms of violation over the civilian population and those held captive. The KLA recognises and respects the international acts of the United Nations and the Conventions on war." My question is: Was that true? Did the KLA recognise and respect the Conventions on war and the international acts of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true that if the KLA did not respect all these documents and norms, it would not have enjoyed the international support.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention now to point number 6 and it reads: "We are in a state of war! We appeal to the Albanian factor to review their attitudes towards the current situation, and make a real judgement. We appeal to the liberation forces to join us at the war front against the enemy. The frustrated and cowardly who try to completely throw our people into defeatism and anarchy should leave as soon as possible. We appeal to the government of Kosovo to unblock the funds collected for the national liberation." My question with respect to this paragraph is: Did you in fact believe that you were in a state of war?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in a state of war even earlier. Now the war had already begun and it was known to all the public opinion in Kosovo and abroad, the international opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could now draw your attention to point 8 in this document where it reads: "We appeal to the Albanian media for an objective presentation of the reality in war. The KLA does not need public promotion and publications for beneficiary aims, nor does it need the denial and distortion of its war." Could you tell us briefly what you -- what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Kosova -- Kosova was occupied by Belgrade and in fact there were media in Albanian in Kosova, both electronic and press, but the media were scared to reflect the reality in Kosovo due to the violence and police monitoring of these media. We didn't have any other media, therefore we appealed as we appealed to all the people, we appealed to those who led the media to inform correctly about the political and military developments in Kosova at that time, and this was a legitimate right of the KLA political and military leaders. In other words, we appealed in order for them to inform the public correctly about what was happening in Kosova, about the terror and genocide that the Belgrade regime was exercising in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you also by this sentence or these sentences seek accurate reporting in the Albanian media about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We appealed for them to inform not only for the KLA, but for all the political and military developments in Kosova because the public opinion in the country and abroad was not getting informed properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd ask that this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be P142.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I want to put before you the last document which you provided to us and which we did not have before you provided it to us, which is -- it is a statement by you dated -- published in Bujku on the 28th of July, 1998. And -- it's two pages. And my first question is: Is this an accurate account of the statement that you made on that date or shortly before that date? And I -- just so we're clear, it's -- appears to be Political Statement Number 5 of the KLA General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did this come from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was issued by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the beginning of the declaration where it states: "As of mid-July, the Belgrade occupying forces have undertaken one of their major offensives after the Second World War in the wider region of Kosovo, with the aim of eliminating the Kosovo Liberation Army from the political scene and submit them to the so-called moderate elements, and to impose an insignificant and defeatist solution on the Albanian people in general, especially the Albanians of Kosovo." Is this a reference to the offensive, the Serb offensive which started at some point in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then I'd like to just draw your attention to the end of the document where it states -- it's on the last page of the English translation and on the second page, near the end, in the Albanian: "We appeal to the international community to seriously, not declaratively, warn Belgrade not to harm the civilian population, to support the just liberation war, which is protected by all international conventions of peace and war, while at the same time condemning the fascist Belgrade regime, which only understands the language of force." My only question is this, what I've just read is: Did you in fact believe that war was protected by all international conventions of peace and war?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could repeat the question. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in the declaration you state that the "just liberation war is protected by all international conventions of peace and war." Do you see that in the document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you mean -- what is meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of people of Europe and of the world in general have gone through the process of liberation wars. This was nothing new or extraordinary for the citizens of Kosova. We were at that time and even today convinced that our war was just, that our war was waged against a regime that now is tried by this Tribunal as well. This was a regime that the international community punished even militarily during the bombing that lasted for 72 days from April till 10th of June, 1999. In this case, the international community defended a nation from extermination, defended a nation from a regime that exercised genocide, the regime of Milosevic, and the Albanian nation is grateful to all the NATO nations who accelerated the process of freedom for the citizens of Kosova and put an end to the most barbaric and violate regime in Europe after that of Hitler in Germany during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P143.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, when we broke on Friday we were going through some public statements that you made in your capacity as spokesman of the Kosovo Liberation Army. And I'd ask now that we turn to -- in the English it's tab 1, 8580. And in the Albanian it's tab 2, 1603 to 1606. And we have the large format for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And for the record this is an interview published in Koha Ditore with Mr. Krasniqi on the 11th of July, 1998, on pages 8 and 9, and then following on the 12th of July on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, is -- did you in fact give an interview to Koha Ditore at this time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the account of the interview that is published here and in the Albanian it's 16 -- U008-1603 to 1606, published over a period -- two different days. Is -- have you had a chance -- have you had an opportunity to read the account of the interview published in Koha Ditore on those two days?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the interview and it was published later; there was no need for me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, have you had a chance to read it to determine if it's accurate, if it's an accurate account of what you said during the interview?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I said in the interview which was published in Koha Ditore newspaper is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could first look at the second page of the Albanian, which is 1604, U008-1604. There's a picture of you seated and there's two individuals standing. Could you tell us first, who are those two people? And --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two persons are Shukri Buja and Nazmi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if I could draw your attention to -- in the Albanian it's the second column on the first page. If you could go back to the first page, 1603, it may be -- and in the second column on the Albanian almost at the bottom, it's the end of your response in the second column. And in the English it's at the top of 8581. And it states -- it states: "The UCK is a liberation army and a regular military formation. It is not an organisation or group that goes in for small-scale actions. Our operations are rather larger, and bear greater resemblance to those of a regular army." Do you see where it says that, Mr. Krasniqi? It's the bottom of the second column in the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question for you is: Was that true, what you said there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even during the last session I stated that this material is a material that is part of the materials used for propaganda purposes. It's something meant to communicate with the public and has appealed to the public. By means of this material, we sought to convey the idea even though sometimes we exaggerated the reality, but the purpose was to win over the support of the citizens of Kosova, to win over the support of the entire Albanian public as well as that of the international public. So as I said, this is a material which aimed at presenting the level of organisation of the KLA at a higher level, which was not the case in reality. That's why I said earlier and will repeat it now that this material aimed at presenting a higher level of organisation for the KLA to enhance the confidence of the members themselves, their trust in victory, as well as the trust of the citizens of Kosova in this victory who were fed up with robbery. So they could no longer put up with the reality. So, Distinguished Judges, I would kindly ask you to look at this interview as well as many other statements issued by the KLA General Staff in this light.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. So is it then your testimony that what is stated here, that the UCK bears a greater resemblance to those of the -- or rather, the actions, the operations, of the UCK bear greater resemblance to those of a regular army, is it your testimony that that was not true and that that was just propaganda?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact what is being presented here was not the will of the General Staff of the KLA, because until March and April of 1998 the KLA was a guerrilla army. And from this state it was transformed into a broader formation because the Serb military and police were taking revenge on the civilian population. Therefore, the KLA was forced to give up the guerrilla warfare and take up positions to protect the civilian population. If you look at it from this point of view, if you look at the actions it carried out on the ground in its clashes with the Serb army and police, they were more similar to the war waged by a regular army. At this time the KLA was in fact a voluntary army, because for an army to be transformed from a guerrilla army into a regular army with the standards required to -- of a regular army was impossible because at this time we were developing horizontally as the KLA with the participation of several categories of people, people - as I said earlier but I need to repeat it again - people who were trained -- prepared to fight against the Serb army and police. After March and April, people joined the KLA to show their solidarity to fight the enemy. At this time we see that the villagers began to be armed even with hunting guns to stay guard in their own villages, and the KLA General Staff started to negotiate, to talk, with all these groups and formations that voluntarily and sometimes out of fear joined the KLA. So the General Staff which was -- had a limited number of persons tried to organise this large mass of people who were willing to fight the Serb army and police and to wage the war so that the Serbian police and army were not fighting against the civilian population. This was very dangerous situation for the General Staff to be able to channel the support of the armed people into the right direction so that their commitment and struggle were not in vain. It was not an easy task. I want to compare it with the situation now. We have the Kosova Protection Corps. For six years now, Kosova is living in new circumstances. Please, I have one more explanation. For six years, despite the attempts of the international community, despite the investments by the donors, the training given to the Kosova Protection Corps, they still have not managed to attain the required standards despite this support and be considered a regular army as required by the international community and the EU. That's why I think that the Honourable Judges should look at the efforts made to transform the KLA into an army typical of the other developed countries in a very peculiar way, because after all I think that at that time we are talking the KLA were the most regular and most disciplined army with the necessary hierarchy, but it was impossible in those circumstances of war to do that, in the circumstances when the army -- the Serb army and police in Kosova had over 50.000 troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the -- just after the beginning of the third column on the Albanian, I'm going to draw your attention to another sentence and it's about a quarter of the way down on the English 8581. It says: "The UCK General Staff had its say before the elections in Kosova, and firmly took the view that the elections should not be held in time of war, because a part of Kosova was in flames." And I have a specific question with respect to this sentence and that is: What elections are being referred to here? When were elections held that the KLA said should not be held?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the elections held in Kosova in March after the massacre committed in Likoshan, Qirez on 28th of February and the 1st of March and after the war waged in Prekaz on the 5th, 6th, and 8th March, 1998. So it's about seven, eight days after these massacres perpetrated by the Serb police and army that elections, free elections, were held in Kosova, which in fact were not free. But even as they were, they were not held all over the territory of Kosova because at that time Serbia had established an iron encirclement in Kosova. So these elections were not held to resolve the Kosova question; they were held to legitimise the Belgrade -- terrorist Belgrade regime. And the KLA, of course, was convinced that nothing new would come of these elections that no parliament would be construed, and that no institutions would be built as the case is even -- as the case was in reality. So we appealed to the population not to be deceived and taken in by such election which could not be held under the boots under the Serb occupiers who were killing innocent people. And we appealed to the people, telling them that such elections should be held because nothing good would come of them, which in fact happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Mr. Whiting. I've just been alerted that with regard to an answer that was had on the previous page there may be a question about the translation, and specifically page 14, line 12. And it's my understanding that Mr. Krasniqi said that he wished that it were the KLA was the most disciplined army. I'm just alerting everybody to this point so that we'll have the transcript double-checked to make sure about this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's an interpreter's mistake. The counsel is right. He said "I wish it were."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the interpreter for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And me, too. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, if I could just draw your attention. In this article there are a number of statements that are made about Mr. Rugova and I'm just going to point them out and then I think we've heard statements like this in other documents but I just want to go through them quickly. On page 8582 of the English -- and it's the bottom of the fifth column on the Albanian it says: "One thing must be made clear: We call him a president even though in many ways he did not deserve the name." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And I believe from the question you're referring there to President Rugova. And then in the next column at the bottom where your last answer and the next column begins. In the English it's about two-thirds of the way down the wage you say: "We consider that Ibrahim Rugova has committed a series of political mistakes to the detriment of national cause, starting from the agreement on education, which came to nothing." And then shortly after that it states: "He is the main divisive factor." And then turning to the next page, 8583 of the English and on the Albanian it's on the next page, 1604. It's on the second page of the article, Mr. Krasniqi, if you just want to see where it is. The bottom of the first column in Albanian says: "Rugova is a pacifist, and he is often said to believe in 'Gandhism.' He is not a pacifist but a doormat. Rugova will not allow resistance but only subservience, letting yourself be trampled underfoot. We have lost our dignity as individuals, families, and a nation. This is true of one-half of the nation. The philosophy of the UCK is to restore to this people their human, family, and national dignity, and to respond to the enemy's barbaric violence with a liberation struggle." And then at the bottom of 8583 and in the Albanian it's the fourth column of 1604 it says: "The UCK expected that Rugova's peaceful policy with the help of the international community, would produce its own results. We've been waiting for 17 years. During this time, the Albanian people have carried out peaceful resistance. But neither Belgrade nor the international community has listened to this voice of the Albanians. Our people have now taken up arms to fight." Now, we've had considerable testimony already from you about Mr. Rugova. My only question is: Do these statements that I have read out and pointed out to you, do they accurately reflect your views of -- about Mr. Rugova's policies at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whatever was read here I think is meant to present not a realistic picture of the situation that prevailed at that time in Kosova. It is a great truth that then and now Ibrahim Rugova has been an opponent, our political opponent, then and now. I have never reconciled and will never reconcile to the policy of subservience and to the Belgrade regime that was pursued then. I want to explain this, Honourable Chamber, that the Kosova Liberation Army was not formed to fight the policy of Ibrahim Rugova. We are political opponents and we are in the same parliament composed of the ruling parties and the opposition. And we do not intend to remove Ibrahim Rugova by force from politics. The KLA has waged the war against the traditional policy of Belgrade occupiers in Kosova. We have not seen the Serbs in Kosova as an obstacle to Kosova. To the KLA all the citizens -- all the violent apparatus of Belgrade met -- established in Kosova -- By means of this I want to say that at no time has the KLA armed itself to take the power, the fictitious power from Rugova's hands because there has never been any other kind of power in Kosova. Therefore, the tendency to present the character of the KLA -- the liberation struggle in Kosova as a struggle between Albanians is unjust. And I think that no citizen in Kosova can accept this and cannot oppose it. I said even during the last session that the Prosecutor is playing up too much the question of the enemy. We didn't fight against that category even though for reasons that are well-known many people have worked in Serb trials, in Serb prosecutors' office in the Serb administration. And even -- they have worked until the June of 1999. We have never dealt with such citizens because most of them -- there are many prosecutors and courts that condemn you twice. They have levelled charges against me. You can see them -- and they still work today in Kosova courts because they are Kosova citizens. Now they work in new circumstances. With this new category of people who were -- and were in the service of that policy, we do not deal with them. They are many. We didn't deal with them during the war either. We in Kosova during the entire period of the liberation war, we fought against the violent apparatus of the Milosevic regime and all those who served that regime in the secret police who have caused harm to the population and who are well-known to the people for what they are done to Kosovo and its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to turn now to the second day of the interview and to the last page that you have before you which should be 1606 at the top. And in the English it -- the second day is at 8586 to 8589. And I'd like to turn to 8589. And, Mr. Krasniqi, I want to ask you about a question and answer which appears. It's not the lasts question and answer but it's the one right before the last question and answer on that last page and I'll just read it out. The question that is put to you by the newspaper is: "The international community has criticised the violation of human rights of Serbian and Montenegrin civilians. What can you say about this?" And your response in the newspaper is: "It does indeed seem to us ridiculous to equate the operations of the UCK with those of the Serb occupier, which are notorious throughout the world. On this it seems to me that the international community is not respecting its conventions, starting with the UN charter, et cetera, because the UCK has never dealt with civilians, or only if they have been in the service of the army and police and done serious harm to the people and the Albanian national cause. There have been cases in which they have been kidnapped, but in this event they have been handed over to international organisations, of course when they have been innocent. First of all, all Serbian forces, whether the police, the military, or armed civilians, are our enemy. From the start, we had our own internal rules for operations. These clearly lay down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Convention [sic] and the conventions governing the conduct of war, even though it has not been offered the chance of signing them, as it would have done. We do not go in for kidnapping. Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians. We do not deal with civilians, and we return those whom we take as prisoners of war. A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross. Those we have kidnapped are either announced in a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." First of all I want to ask you about what you say in this answer about the "internal rules for our operations," which "clearly lay down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Convention and the conventions governing the conduct of war." Were those rules written down at this time? Did you have written rules that you're referring to here?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The International Red Cross has sent us some concrete documents which the KLA should respect these Conventions. It was a document that we circulated at that time; that's why we say here that the KLA has not dealt with civilians. The civilians who have been seized by the KLA have been handed over to the International Red Cross and the representatives of the Red Cross that were present in Kosova at that time might prove what I'm saying better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The documents that were provided to the KLA from the International Red Cross, were these then converted into a document from the UCK and then circulated or did you just circulate the documents that you had received from the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We circulated the documents and respected them. I think that all international mechanisms that were present in Kosova at that time, be them of the humanitarian area like Red Cross or political and diplomatic area which were in Kosova then, they -- We had frequent contacts with the representatives of the international community and because we respected the international documents on citizens, we were supported by the international community. Because as KLA, as armed people, we could have organised attacks on Serb population and villages in many parts of Kosova, but all over the time -- during all the time of the war, this has never happened, even in a single instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To whom did you circulate these documents? Who received them?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Red Cross has distributed these documents on the grass roots. It's not that we have always managed to maintain regular links with all the units, because the presence of the Serb police and army was so great that we couldn't. And the areas controlled by the KLA were limited or were not many at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were soldiers -- was there some mechanism for soldiers in the KLA to be made aware -- either given these documents or made aware of what was said in these documents?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's difficult for the Trial Chamber to imagine how the KLA was organised at that time, how spread out it was. Also because of the fact that the Serb police and army attacks were almost daily. In these circumstances, for us it was not possible to send these documents to every single soldier. So the people were informed through statements, through communiques. As I said, we didn't have the possibilities to write and distribute them in a written form because that was the time when we didn't have even a single PC.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, there is a reference at the end of the passage that I read to you. It says: "A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross." Do you know who that's referring to?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information -- I don't know who they were, but I had information that two Serbs who were captured, and they were from Croatia, were handed over to the International Red Cross. I was unable to be in every spot when people who were captured were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember anything -- hearing anything about Ivan and Vojko Bakrac being turned over to the Red Cross on July 6th, 1998, four days before this interview? Do you remember hearing anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I remember that they were handed over, but those names that you mentioned I had the opportunity to see them only as witnesses of the Prosecution here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you don't remember those names from the time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn now, please, to tab 7 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'll ask the assistance of the usher for the witness. For the record, this is an article dated 2 September 1998 which is -- the head line, at least in the English version is: "Demaqi Speaks on Position of Liberation Army." The English version is from FBIS, it's two pages long. It's Albanian version is U008-6947.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I would draw your attention to the article there at the top of the page by Bardh Rugova. I think it's been provided in an easier-to-read format now. Mr. Krasniqi, at this time in September of 1998 can you tell us who Adem Demaqi was?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adem Demaqi was the political representative of the KLA in Pristina. His duty was to unite the leaders of the political bodies that were active in Pristina in order to unite them and create a national assembly which would take responsibility to lead institutionally the war and the political processes that were going on at the time in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to -- I think it's the fifth paragraph or so. It states -- at least in the English it is. It states: "The UCK's political representative," referring to Adem Demaqi, "also talked about his meeting at the Supreme Staff of the UCK with its spokesman Jakup Krasniqi." And then quoting from Mr. Demaqi: "'I discussed with him a list drawn up of the International Red Cross of people considered lost, knowing that the Supreme Staff is against actions of this kind. They (the UCK) promised that they would distribute the list for investigation by the local staffs, because desperate people may have lost all feeling and acted against this basic standpoint.'" And that's the end of the quotation and the article continues: "Demaqi added that he did not rule out such a thing having happened." Mr. Krasniqi, do you recall this thing happening, Mr. Demaqi meeting with you and giving you a list from the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it would have been better to ask Demaqi about this, but to my recollection of course during the war I had contacts with Adem Demaqi, since he was the political representative in Pristina, with the duty that I mentioned earlier. He did bring a list to the General Staff, and we distributed that list in the zones of the Kosova Liberation Army. However, it was not stated on that list the place or time when and where those people were taken. Due to the bad communication that we had with certain parts of the KLA, we were not able to determine that these people were captured by organised units of the KLA. And of course I told him that these names did not exist and that the KLA had no knowledge of these names. Here I would like to clarify and explain another thing. I am convinced that the Belgrade regime had infiltrated within its ranks unarmed people as well. And these people of course might have gotten killed during combat between the KLA and the Serb armed forces. And for the Serbian regime of Milosevic to justify its victims before their families, the regime would call these people missing or killed. This was the morale [as interpreted] of that regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that you distributed the list in the zones of the Kosovo Liberation Army, can you tell us more specifically what you did to distribute the list. Did you distribute it to zone commanders, to brigade commanders, battalion commanders? How did you distribute the list?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list was distributed through the couriers that existed within the ranks of the KLA, designated persons who were to deliver the post. There was no other way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. But who received the list to your knowledge? In other words, who was the list sent to? You said it was distributed in the zone --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lists were usually sent to the zones and the zones then were to convey those lists to its units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you didn't -- you received no information back from the zones about the people who were identified on the list. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd ask to turn, please, to tab 8 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in the -- And in the -- this is an article -- an interview with Jakup Krasniqi in Koha Ditore published on the 2nd of September, 1998, on page 3. The English translation is from FBIS and is four pages. And the Albanian is ERN U008-6946.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you see that interview?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you give this interview to Koha Ditore?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to a passage which in the English is on the third page of the translation, and it's the -- in the Albanian it's not the last answer that you give, Mr. Krasniqi, in the interview, but it's the one right before the last answer. So I think it's -- well, I'll read it and see if you're able to find it. "We do not know anything about the imprisonment or" -- this is you speaking. "We do not know anything about the imprisonment of any kidnapping of any Serbian journalists or citizens. The UCK has not taken up weapons to fight against Serbian journalists and citizens, but to fight against Serbian soldiers and terrorists that have reduced Kosova to ashes. After all the terror and devastation that have been seen in Kosova, it is impossible to keep under control the feelings of hatred and vengeance that the enemy himself has inspired. Despite our insistence that the Albanians' struggle must not resemble the barbarism practiced by the enemy." Do you see that answer in the interview, Mr. Krasniqi? Are you able to find that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what you just read differs a lot from that what is in Albanian. So I will try to read it in Albanian. "We don't know anything about the imprisonment or kidnapping of any Serbian journalist or citizen. The KLA has not taken up arms to fight against Serbian journalists and citizens but to fight against Serbian soldiers and terrorists that have reduced Kosova to ashes. After all the terror and devastation seen in Kosova, it is impossible to keep under control the feelings of hatred and vengeance that the enemy himself has inspired. Despite our insistence that our struggle must not resemble the barbarism practiced by the enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. My only question is: What did you mean when you said "it is impossible to keep under control the feelings of hatred and vengeance that the enemy himself has inspired"?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So we are speaking of a time when we could freely say that the offensive undertaken by the Serb police and army was coming to an end. The Serb forces had undertaken an offensive throughout the territory of Kosova and particularly in the Drenica municipalities in the Pastrik municipalities and in the major part of the Dukagjini zone. The entire Kosova was in flames and we were defending. We were defending the population, the civilian population, which was a continuous target for the Serbian police and army. Villages were in flames. As I said in the previous session, during this offensive over 450 settlements, Albanian settlements, came out burnt and devastated. And despite all this terror, devastation, and burning to the ground that the Serbian forces exercised, I am honoured to say that the KLA never took revenge on the Serbian civilians. And there is no -- nothing that could argue this fact. This is what I wanted to say: that perhaps individual deeds by members who were not members of the KLA, these people might have not controlled their own feelings; and we had no knowledge of these acts, not at that time and not even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it your testimony then that during the war not a single member of the KLA committed a single crime?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that to the knowledge of the political and military leaders of the KLA, it did not happen. This is what I want to say and I say this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it a convenient time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I just have one more article to ask you about and it's at tab 9. And it's from Koha Ditore and I'll need the assistance of the usher, please. At tab 9 it's -- perhaps the witness has already found it. It is an article from Koha Ditore from the 4th of November, 1998, on page 7. The Albanian is U008-6943. And on the Albanian -- Mr. Krasniqi, we'll provide a large copy of it; that should be easier to read. In the Albanian I would draw your attention to the middle of the page on the left. Do you see that? It's a statement from the Military Police Directorate and I think it's number 4. And I'd just like to -- I'll just read out -- it's a brief statement and I'll just read it out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreters have a very small print copy and they can't read it in Albanian. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have another big version of it that we can provide to the interpreters with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It says: "Statement issued by the Military Police Directorate of the Kosovo Liberation Army in Pristina on 1 November. "On 30 October, the Military Police of the Operational Subzone of Pastrik arrested Jakup Kastrati of the village of Turjake near Malisheve [Malisevo], the chairman of the Malisheve Branch of the Democratic League in Kosova [LDK], and Cen Desku from the village of Siceve, resident in Malisheve, the LDK branch's deputy chairman. The directorate of the UCK Intelligence Service possesses data about their activity against the UCK's liberation struggle. These persons have spread propaganda for the surrender of weapons in collusion with the collaborationists Selman Binici from the village of Baje and Ramiz Hoxha from Bellanice, who have been both been executed by the UCK, and are in ongoing cooperation with the LDK Presidium Member Agim Krasniqi, known to the UCK Intelligence Service as an agent of covert operations against the UCK and the initiator of a kind of policy of autonomy for Kosova. "The Investigation Department of the UCK Military Police Directorate are conducting investigations of the arrested men Jakup Kastrati and Cen Desku in Remand Prison No. 3." Now, this does not purport to the a communique from the General Staff or a statement by you, but in your capacity as spokesman of the KLA, were you aware of this statement from the Military Police Directorate of the UCK?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You did not see this statement at the time it was issued?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see this at the time it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear anything at that time? Did you receive any information at that time about the arrest of Jakup Kastrati and Cen Desku?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could first answer the question and then you -- I welcome your clarification, but if you could first answer: Did you hear anything at the time about the arrest of Jakup Kastrati and Cen Desku?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would note that one microphone of the witness is turned off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know more about their release than their arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special war was mentioned here. It is true that at that time special war was waged by certain individuals and not only those people who are armed -- who had joined the army, but there were civilians as well because there were even in the KLA there were former officers of the Yugoslav army who had been part of the Secret Service of the Yugoslav army. There were people who had been punished or charged with criminal offences. And I would say like to say that after the summer offensive these people, they were -- they handed over to the enemy 5.000 or 6.000 weapons. It is well-known, for example, the instance when weapons were handed over in the Dukagjini area by Tahir Zema. This handing over of weapons continued at a smaller scale in the Istog municipality in the Therande municipality. And there were people who asked for handing over -- the handing over of guns in Malisevo. And this was done by Januz Kastrati and Cen Desku. And in the beginning it was suspected that these had made an appeal to several soldiers to hand over their weapons. Speaking to them about the lack of prospect of this war. And of course, the soldiers of the KLA apprehended these individuals, kept them in prison, I don't know for how long, but I know that from the 25th to the 27th of November they were kept in prison. And then at the request of diplomatic representatives in Kosovo with whom we communicated, more concretely with the American ambassador in Skopje, Chris Hill, and the EU ambassador. And these two people together with two Serb journalists who were captured in the area between Goles and Fushtice, a village in the municipality of Drenoc. So these four people were handed over to the international representatives in the presence of the International Red Cross. But it could be around the 25th or the 27th of November, 1998. I'm not very sure about the date, but it must have been those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, who in the KLA was involved in either the arrest or the release of these individuals, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know -- I said all I know about it. I can't add anything else to what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The article also refers to the execution of Selman Benici from Baje and Ramiz Hoxha from Bellanice. Did you hear anything about that happening at the time? Were you informed about that as KLA spokesman and member of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the word "execution" here has been used in another sense of the word. They must have been killed according to the information I had, but they were -- they were giving information to the force -- to the Serbian forces in Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made a reference in your last answer or one of your last answers to Tahir Zema. Where, if you know, did Tahir Zema operate in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tahir Zema operated in the operational zone of Dukagjini, zone number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the months of May, June, and July of 1998, do you know who the commander of the Drenica zone was?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you mean the Dukagjini zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I'm changing subjects. I meant the Drenica zone. Who was the commander of the Drenica zone?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sulejman Selimi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to change subjects again and go back to your first declaration, first public declaration as spokesman of the KLA and I'm going to ask for the assistance of Mr. Younis. I'm going to show you a clip from a video that's in evidence in this case. It's from P034, and it's clip -- our clip number 5. I just ask you, Mr. Krasniqi, to watch the computer and I'm going to pause it at a certain moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "At this time Shala family's kulla was the headquarters of the KLA General Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you see the image in front of you, yourself and two men standing on either side of you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although it's a poor image, I can see that it's a picture of me and two of me comrades, co-fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the date on the image there is 14 June 1998, which from your earlier testimony I believe is the date that you made your first public declaration as spokesman of the KLA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this in fact an image of you making that declaration?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'd ask the usher, please, if you can ensure that computer evidence is pressed on his monitor. It is. Just -- because there will be a clearer image and the witness has suggested that it's not very clear. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us who the people are standing on either side of you, on the right and on the left.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of them is Fatmir Limaj and the other one is Ferat Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's Fatmir Limaj on the right in the image?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I see it. It's on -- he is on my right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, to be clear, he's on the right of the image. As you look at the screen, he's on the right of the image you see. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's on my right in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's a little unclear and it may be a translation problem. Who is standing closest to the flag?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ferat Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us where this was filmed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was filmed in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, the image is, as I said, from P034 and it's -- on the timing, it's at 16:55:1, 16 minutes, 55 seconds. And I think we can take that down. At this time --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You can take it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At this time on the 14th of June of 1998, where was the General Staff located?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clarified this in the previous session, but I will repeat it. At this time the General Staff did not have a given headquarters. Because of the war situation and for security reasons, we moved from one place to another. And this image that was taken in Klecka, in fact we went there -- we went to the Berisa Mountains where the village is, for security reasons, only to make this video, and then we left -- we went to other areas. And every time we had these videos made, some of them were made in this kulla, in this place in Klecka. So I repeat, we did them there for security reasons, not because Klecka was the headquarters of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said the General Staff would move from village to village for security reasons. What other villages would this -- the General Staff move to during this time period in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In -- during this period the General Staff went from my village to Malisheve in some cases, to Divjake, and we went to other villages as well, villages of Drenica, to Vrboc and to Lladroc, and in the villages around the mountainous area -- the mountainous area of Berisa, such as Kroimire and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At that time this statement was made by you on the 14th of June, 1998, what was Fatmir Limaj's pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were any fighting units named after him?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know it was the unit that Fatmir led in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The unit in Klecka to your knowledge was called the Celiku unit?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And to your knowledge it was named the Celiku unit after him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there must be a point when leading questions stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I haven't objected so far today. Perhaps it's about time I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that he's just -- I'm clarifying his answer. He's already answered that question, but I'm just clarifying it. He said yes. And to your knowledge it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the position is one where the precise form of your question is on the wrong side of the line, but you're certainly properly entitled to clarify. If you could try it with a question that isn't leading that would be the way to go, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Celiku unit that -- the Celiku unit in Klecka that was led by Fatmir Limaj, do you know how it got its name?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time all the units operated under different names, various names. So I could not have known why a certain unit got this name or that name, and that was not my responsibility in the long run. This was something that up to the operational segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think you've answered the question. At that time on the 14th of June, 1998, what was -- do you know what Fatmir Limaj's position was?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you've told us that he led this Celiku unit in Klecka. Was he the highest commander in Klecka, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I just knew him, Fatmir I mean. And that because of this public appearance that I had to make from Klecka at the time. I just knew him. I did not have any other contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- you've told us that he was commander of a unit called the Celiku unit in Klecka. Was there a -- do you know if there was any commander above him in Klecka or was he the highest commander in Klecka?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Klecka, Ismet Jashari was another one who had a commanding position as well, but I did not know at the time who of these two had the highest position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the statement on the 14th of June, 1998, do you know where Fatmir Limaj went in the following days after that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was wartime and people would not want to know where they went or we did not want to know where other people went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it your answer that you did not know where he went in the days after the 14th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that, yes. But also another thing, that I never wanted other people to know where I was going so I never asked other people where they were going because, as I said, it was wartime and unpleasant things could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the months of -- well, let me ask you this first: On the 14th of June, 1998, was this the first time that you had seen Fatmir Limaj in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the first time I met him. And we did not speak at length to each other, but we had thought that in my first public appearance there should be two soldiers and they are Fatmir Limaj, who was based in Klecka with his unit, his military unit, and on the other side, close to the flag, was Ferat Shala from the Pellumbi unit. He's from the other side of the Lapusnik village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say "the other side of the Lapusnik village," is that the other side of the Peja-Pristina road?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right side of the Pristina-Peja road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On the right side going in which direction, towards Peja or towards Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, during the months -- after the 14th of June, 1998, until the end of July 1998, did you ever see Fatmir Limaj in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in Malisheve -- I have seen him there, but we did not have time to have a conversation with each other because of the tasks we had -- each of us had to fulfil within the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During that time period, how many times did you see him in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember how many times I saw him in Malisheve, but I remember one other meeting with European Union representatives in Klecka. I can't remember whether it was July or August. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that meeting in just a moment, but before I do -- can you remember approximately how many times you saw him in Malisevo between June 14th and the end of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I can't say how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No idea? No approximate -- you can't approximate at all? Three? Five? Ten? 20?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. When I say I can't remember, I can't say whether it was once or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific -- any one specific occasion you saw him in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During that time period did you see him in any other village?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many times did you see him in Klecka, again during the time period of from the 14th of June, 1998, to the end of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be three or four. I did not take the number down, but it was not very often that I met him because each of us had their own tasks to fulfil within the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from Malisheve and Klecka, did you see him in any other village during that time period?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During May, June, and July of 1998, did you yourself ever go to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During those months, do you know who the commander of -- who the commander was in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you made reference to a meeting you had in Klecka either in July or August of 1998 with the European Union. Do you remember who it is you met with?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember but maybe I'll get confused with the names. Maybe if I could refer to the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us specifically what it is that you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I spoke about this in the first statement I made in Pristina. I mentioned the names, but now I don't seem to remember their names. I know that one of them was a witness here before this Tribunal. I think Ditman [phoen] was either the name or the surname of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me see if I can assist you with this in helping you remember the names. Okay. I draw your attention to paragraph 46 of your statement and see if that refreshes your recollection with respect to the names.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were three of them in fact. Jan Kickert, David Slinn, and the third one, Ditman. While on our side was me, Ram Buja, and Mr. Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection with respect to the date of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You can put that away for now. Now, you've said on your side it was Fatmir Limaj, yourself, and Ram Buja. Who was Ram Buja at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ram Buja was the person responsible to organise the civil authorities, the civil power, in the free areas. And after that, he became a member of the General Staff of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where were the free areas at that time? I mean, I know that the offensive has just begun, but when you say he was responsible for organising the civil authorities in the free areas, what areas are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the areas where the KLA was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that all the areas where the KLA present all over Kosovo or in only a certain part of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the -- of Kosovo -- I mean the areas where -- which were under the control of the KLA. For example, in Drenica; part of Dukagjini; part of Pastrik; and between the municipality of Mitrovica and Vushtrri, the area of Shala i Bajgora. But there were other areas as well that were under KLA control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And at this time, the 30th of July, 1998, what was Fatmir Limaj's position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember anything else except the fact that he was there with his unit in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, why was he at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. Why was Fatmir Limaj at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in this meeting because we had this meeting with representatives of the Council of Europe and there were only two people from the General Staff. So we needed, of course, to have other people in that meeting. And at that moment, the person with a highest education and professional preparation was Fatmir. So we asked him to be present in that meeting; also because the situation was very serious. Enemy attacks -- we were receiving enemy attacks from all sides. So that's why we thought it necessary for him to be present in that meeting because the meeting was also held in the area where Fatmir and his unit were based.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At that time, on the 30th of July, 1998, was Malisevo still under the control of the UCK or had it fallen to the Serb control, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly the fall of Malisevo, when it happened, but I thought it was after the Malisevo -- Malisevo fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember what was discussed at this meeting with Jan Kickert and David Slinn and the third person you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember something, not many concrete things about it, but I think we discussed also about the creation of a delegation of Albanians from Kosovo that would be made up of -- from various political subjects and representatives of the KLA. This delegation would have to present to the international factor its own demands in a coordinated way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else that was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the essence of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would it further refresh your recollection about the meeting to look again at the notes you referred to earlier, the paragraph 46 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will look at them, but I don't think it will bring something more to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just ask you to read through the paragraph and see -- it's a brief paragraph -- see if it refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course we discussed and informed the representatives of the European Council that the KLA recognises the conventions, the international conventions of war and respects them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall Fatmir Limaj saying anything during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time now. Many things happened, this traumatic things happened after that. But mainly it was I who spoke on that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the meeting, did you have any discussion with Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have time to continue because of our duties, because, I will say it again, it's a time when the Serb offensive was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want show you a photograph which is at tab 11 of the binder. And it's -- for the record it's from Prosecution Exhibit P24. And it's ERN U003-3240. You can either look on the photograph on the screen or you can look at it in the binder in front of you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the people in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From right to left can you tell us who they are?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj, Rexhep Selimi, and myself, Jakup Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think there was from left to right, but in any event. Do you remember when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, on the right on the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there will be any confusion about this point, but do you remember when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not easy for me to give the precise time; however, this photograph was made after the summer offensive of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise about this either. It's either taken in Shati Idri [phoen] or Novo Selo or in Lladroc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the man in the middle, Rexhep Selimi, what was his position at this time, if you know? At the time the photograph was taken, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before, he had the duty of general inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain a little bit more what was his duty as general inspector. Was he a member of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was his responsibility as general inspector?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: His responsibility was to visit more frequently the war zones and to collect information about the situation in those zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you remember at the time that this photograph was taken what the position of Fatmir Limaj was within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it is difficult for me to give the precise time when this photograph was taken, but I know that it is in November between 11 and 13th of November a long meeting was held of the General Staff and in that meeting Fatmir Limaj became a member of the General Staff. And of course after this time our meetings were more frequent, perhaps even on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I know you can't remember precisely when this photograph was taken, but do you remember if it was before or after Fatmir Limaj became a member of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise about this either, but it should be around this time, maybe after he became a member of the General Staff. But again, I will stress it again, I don't know accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we can take that off the screen how.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a different subject, Mr. Krasniqi, and that is the responsibilities of KLA commanders at whatever level towards the General Staff. And I want to focus for these questions on the time period of June and July of 1998. Now, I know that you have testified that to your knowledge no crimes were committed. My question though, is: If a crime had been -- is a commander of an area learned of a crime being committed by a KLA soldier within his area, did he have any duties to report that crime to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
