utterances.text: Every leader of the operational units, which after September, when we have the formation of the brigade units of the KLA, it was their obligation to inform the General Staff about all the developments in their areas of responsibility. As a General Staff, not in a single case did we receive information that executions of captives were carried out by members of the KLA. Such acts -- about such acts we heard only after the arrest of Fatmir and his friends by the Tribunal and even earlier from certain arrests that were made in Kosovo of former KLA members. I will say it again that as General Staff we didn't have information that someone committed the killing of detained persons. It is true that the General Staff about all the arrests that were made - and there were arrests both of soldiers and civilians - but all these arrested persons were released. And maybe the most known case to the international public was the capturing of eight Serbs in January 1998 in Shala i Bajgora. And later these soldiers after many discussions were exchanged with nine soldiers who had been captured in Guznin [phoen] of Prizren or Djakovica on 15 December 1998. There were other cases as well when people were captured, mainly Serbs, who later, with the mediation of the international factor, were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify you spoke of the release of eight Serbs. I think we had a translation problem. Did that occur in January of 1998 or January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said it was the obligation of every leader of the operational units to inform the General Staff about all developments in their areas of responsibility. Was that true in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained the organisational state in May, June, July of 1998. If there is a need for additional explanation, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. But my question is -- you have told us that there were unit commanders and you've told us about a zone commander Sulejman Selimi in Drenica during May, June, and July of 1998. My question is: At that time, did those commanders have the obligation that you described to inform the General Staff about everything that happened in their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to answer this question it is needed to make an explanation that not in all zones where the KLA was operating, not all of these zones were of a same organisational level. This differed from zone to zone, and depended also on the expansion of the KLA in those relevant zones. For example, in this time we're talking about, the Drenica zone had a better organisation due to the fact that the fighting between the KLA of this zone and the Serb police and military forces had started in November 1997. So the level of organisation in this zone was of a better quality. After the Drenica zone, of a better organisational level for that time we were -- we are speaking about was the Dukagjini operational zone. As for the other zones, including here the Pastrik zone, they lagged behind in organisation. This will change later on and will become of a better quality after the offensive, the summer offensive of 1998. So the level of organisation arose also in Shale which included the municipality of Mitrovica and Vushtrri and the preparation of the forces in the Llap zone of Shala i Bajgora began in the autumn of 1998. A weaker level of organisation in this time was evident in Nerodime zone, while in the beginning of the organisation it was in Karadak zone. So this was the situation at the organisational level of the KLA operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Krasniqi, but that's an answer to a different question I've put to you. The question I have asked you is: During May, June, and July of 1998 did commanders in the KLA have an obligation to inform the General Staff about everything that happened in their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was. However, I mentioned it in the earlier session that in this time the growth of interest of the citizens to join the KLA was very evident in this time and we here have the horizontal layout without the vertical one. And at that time, we mainly dealt with the systemisation of persons who had joined the ranks. We cannot say that the level of responsibility was what you are asking here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just asking questions, sir. I'm going to move to a different topic and that is Rahovec. Are you aware of fighting that occurred in Rahovec in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In July 1998 fighting was not going on solely in Rahovec. There were two battle sites that I would like to explain and clarify. It is the fighting in Rahovec and the fight in Bardhi i Madh for the Obiliq mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to focus on Rahovec. Did --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are interrelated, Rahovec and Bardhi i Madh, so I see a need to explain here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you a few questions and maybe we can explain that. Were you present for the fighting in Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present in the Rahovec fighting because I didn't have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the duty of a soldier or a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember how the fighting started in Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to explain, how the fighting started in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please explain, briefly if you can.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to inform the Judges about the fighting in Rahovec and in Bardhi i Madh. In both cases the fighting began without the authorisation of the General Staff of the KLA, because we, being of an organisational level, we were conscious of our own organisational means in such circumstances and we did not authorise the attack of Rahovec and Bardhi i Madh due to the fact that we lacked weapons that were necessary for the liberation of these towns and we were lacking weapons to keep under control a city of a size of Rahovec or a plain place as was Bardhi i Madh. When the fighting started, the engagement of the General Staff was to help and put under control those military forces, our military forces, that were not fully under the command of the General Staff. And also members of the General Staff took part in the fighting in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which members of the General Staff took part in the fighting in Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Rahovec fighting, the following took part: Kadri Veseli, member of the General Staff, who in fact found himself encircled there and had trouble in getting out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Any other members of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment I can't remember. I do remember that there was another military person who was appointed there to estimate -- assess the level, the organisational level, of the KLA units there. He was killed in Rahovec. His name is Agim Cela.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the date that the fighting started in Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did the fighting start with the KLA attacking or the Serbs attacking or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It could be the town unit of Rahovec, but I don't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the town under the control of the KLA for some time, some period of days?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This control was very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many days?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak in days, but it was a very short time. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. During -- from August 1998 onwards, did you hear anything about detention camps being operated by members of the KLA in the Llap zone, and specifically in Lapashtica, Majac and Potok, or Bajgora, starting in August 1998. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time in the zones that you mentioned there were no operational units of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mean in the Llap zone there was no -- from August 1998 on there were no operational units of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Llap units at that time were based in Shala Bajgora.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so -- is it -- just so we're clear about your testimony, is it your testimony that you know nothing about detention camps being operated by the KLA in the Llap zone from August 1998 onwards?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During May, June, and July of 1998 did you ever meet Isak Musliu, also known as Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about Haradin Bala, also known as Shala? Did you meet him during those months of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither with him. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. I see, Mr. Topolski, you have volunteered once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski will ask some questions of you now, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I do so on behalf of a man you've never met, Isak Musliu, otherwise known as Qerqizi. Can I indicate to you, please, that there are six areas I want to ask you about and I shall indicate what they are. I want to ask you first of all about propaganda; I then want to ask you about collaborators; then detention and arrests; fourthly, structure; fifthly, territorial control or lack of it by the KLA; and sixthly and finally, questions regarding Serbian state security. And I suspect I may take the rest of the day to do it. Mr. Krasniqi, I shall try as best I can to make my questions both short and precise. We'll get along faster, sir, if you're able to make your responses equally short and equally precise. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. So let's start with propaganda. And can I please to begin with venture a definition of propaganda. Propaganda, I suggest is an organised programme of publicity or selected information used to propagate a doctrine or a practice; an organised programme of publicity or selected information used to propagate a doctrine or a practice. Mr. Krasniqi, would you accept that as a working definition of the word "propaganda"?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. Well, you've just agreed with the Oxford reference dictionary, so that's a good start. More importantly, Mr. Krasniqi, may I put this to you: That propaganda is an essential weapon in the armoury of an organisation such as the KLA. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That is particularly so where a volunteer army is involved, as was the case here in Kosova in 1998. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree and I did say this during my speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The purpose of communiques perhaps could be said to have served more than one purpose, but again, would you agree with the proposition that for the most part their primary purpose was propaganda?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's look for a moment or two other purposes that propaganda may serve in the situation that you and your colleagues, comrades, found themselves. Propaganda would be important, would it not, regarding the morale of the civilian population. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It would serve the purpose also of encouraging recruitment into the ranks of the KLA. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Due to the lack of other mobilisation means, the communiques, the statements, and all other public statements were in this purpose in the mobilisation of volunteers into the ranks of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Another purpose, I suggest, would be to talk up successes, talk up military successes. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree -- I agree that we had to speak about success even when there wasn't any success to speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's an interesting answer that follows neatly, I hope, into my next proposition, that another purpose of it was to talk down failures. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had taken up weapons and of course we wanted to speak about victory and not about defeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My next and final proposition regarding the purposes of propaganda, Mr. Krasniqi, would be this: That it was an essential element in psychological warfare. Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, let me move to what I suggest in reality was an example of propaganda at work: The territorial control claimed by the KLA; that's the topic. Could you go, please, to tab 5 of the file that Mr. Whiting was taking you through last week and today. Mr. Krasniqi, I hope this is backed by the Albanian translation of this document which is in fact the text of the Der Speigel interview given by you on the 6th of July. First of all, sir, do you agree that is what we are looking at here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is there a larger copy of this for Mr. Krasniqi of the Der Speigel interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is one where we don't have the newspaper version of it and it's -- the Albanian is ordinary size.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the English should be backed by the Albanian in your file there. Have you got the Albanian translation of it? In text form, not in duplication-of-newspaper form? Is this it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it Exhibit P140? I hear concurrence, as though from your mouth, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course I learned a long time ago to never agree with somebody that comes from either beside one or behind one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have an extra copy of the translation that we can provide to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have mine, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it in there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... maybe Mr. Whiting would be kind enough to provide -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Krasniqi, I will take you to a specific question that I have for you regarding territorial claims of domination by the KLA, but before we get there let's just look together at the first page of this interview and indeed the very first question which reads, and would you follow me, sir, in your own language to ensure that you're looking at an accurate translation. "Q. Mr. Krasniqi, your troops have just suffered a defeat in a battle for the Belasevac coal mine. Nevertheless, you have announced that you plan to conquer the provincial capital of Pristina soon. How and when?" Mr. Krasniqi, have I just read to you an accurate translation of what you see in that document there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the translation is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let's see if they have accurately translated your answer to that question, suggesting that you had plans to conquer Pristina on the 6th of July of 1998. Your answer as translated: "I am very serious about that. We already have a large number of our fighters in place on the way to Pristina. They are just waiting for our signal to attack." Mr. Krasniqi, is there a word of truth in that answer in reality as of the 6th of July, 1998? You know I ask the question, sir, respectfully. Indeed, did you have a large number of fighters in place waiting for your signal to attack Pristina or is that propaganda? You're smiling.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course my answer is -- was what is here in the interview. We didn't take up weapons just to stay in the mountains of Kosovo. Our purpose was to liberate Kosova. Although the means of organisation and growth were limited, I had to say what I said at that time for the opinion, public opinion, in Kosova. So the purpose was to bring some hope within the population of Kosovo who were fed up with the Belgrade regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in my country we have an expression, maybe in yours, too: That there are lies, there are damned lies, and there are statistics. May we add a fourth to that, there are lies, there are damned lies, there are statistics, and then there's propaganda. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Topolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I couldn't beat it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, could we please go to what in the English anyway is the second page of that document. What I'm looking for is a Der Speigel question that is about five or six questions after the one we've just looked at and begins with the words "Aren't you overestimating your troops' fighting strength?" Could you be good enough to find a question that begins like that.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The question in full is, and would you be good enough to check the translation as I read: "Aren't you overestimating your troops' fighting strength? They do not have a chance against the Yugoslav army." And your response is this: "Nowadays we are getting enough weapons and we also have antiaircraft missiles. We control 40 per cent of the country. There are more than 5 million Albanians in the Balkans who will help each other in the moment of danger." Mr. Krasniqi, first of all are those words that I've just read in English the same in the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to ask you only about two, or I should say three, actually, parts of that answer. Would you bear in mind that you are here speaking to Der Speigel on the 6th of July, 1998. Were you "getting enough weapons" in July 1998, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time far from having sufficient or enough weapons, less so did we have anti-aircraft missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, thank you for the composite answer to the question. You anticipated my next question, so I'll just move on to the third. Mr. Krasniqi, this is important because evidence this Tribunal has already heard appears to accord with what you're saying to Der Speigel. "We control 40 per cent of the country." Again, Mr. Krasniqi, was that precise figure that you gave to Der Speigel accurate as of the 6th of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When you were answering questions a short while ago this afternoon from Mr. Whiting, you were being shown a document - and I'm not going to take you to it but the reference ends 38589 - and it's a document that is dated the 12th of July, communique I think. In speaking about that document, Mr. Krasniqi, to us on your oath this afternoon you describe the area controlled by the KLA as being limited; page 21, line 15 of the transcript. Assume, as I do of course, that that answer you gave this afternoon is an accurate one and an honest one, it tends to confirm, does it not, that you were doing nothing more than propagandising when you were speaking to Der Speigel on the 6th of July, 1998. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to see if I can focus on that very same period of time with you for a moment, please. And I appreciate that I'm not asking you questions as a military man, but as a political man at the time of these events. Do you remember an attack by the KLA on the town of, and forgive my pronunciation, sir, I hope I'm right, Orahovac on the 18th of July, 1998? Do you recall that attack?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a paper written and produced by the ICG called Kosovo's Long Hot Summer, a briefing on military, humanitarian, and political developments in Kosovo? Do you recollect such a document?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The KLA attacked Orahovac on the 18th of July, did it not, and I suggest the case is the Serbian police re-established control of Orahovac just four days later on the 22nd of July. Does that accord with your recollection of these events, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answers I said I don't remember the date -- the dates, how many days. Because it wasn't long from the moment that Rahovec was taken over by the KLA and the attacks by the Serb forces. Maybe it was three, four, maximum five days; it was not a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, is Rahovec, spelled R-a-h-o-v-e-c, the same as a place spelled O-r-a-h-o-v-a-c? Is that the same place?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Orahovac is in Serbian language; Rahovec is in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it right, as I suggest be the case, that after the fall of Orahovac on or about the 22nd of July back into Serb control, they pushed on, did the Serbs, and took the headquarters of the KLA in Malisevo on the 29th of July. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be sometime by the end of July. I don't remember an accurate time. Certainly the document you have in mind must show the accurate date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But they pushed on and re-took KLA headquarters in Likovac on the 6th of August and Junik on the 15th of August, otherwise known as the Serb offensive. Do you agree with the dates I put to you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the time of the highest peak of the Serb offensive, and I may agree with the date, but I cannot remember the accurate dates because the situation was very grave at that time. As I mentioned earlier, many villages were in flames, they were being shelled with all sorts of weapons, artillery and otherwise, by the Serb forces. So it's hard for me to remember the accurate dates. But it is a time when one after the other that the seats of the KLA, like Malisheve, Likovc, and then Junik fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We'll come back to look together at one or two other aspects of territorial control, as I indicated to you at the outset a little later, but can I move on still under the heading of propaganda. Mr. Krasniqi, at the time you were appointed to become spokesman of the KLA, had you any media experience? Do you understand what I mean by the question?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Even before I became the spokesperson, I had experience only in writing for the media but not appearing before the media outlets, especially the electronic media, and I didn't give interviews in the past. So in a few words I would say I didn't have experience of working with the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't know if it matters but the witness's other microphone is not switched on. I don't know if that matters or not, but I will point it out. Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. I think this helps for your voice to be heard by all interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The writing that you did for the media, was that of a political nature, of an academic nature, of an entertainment nature or what? What was the writing that you had done before your appointment as spokesman?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote some articles. Also I wrote about academic issues since at that time I was doing post-university studies at Pristina University.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence correctly and accurately to be that you have always been - and I'm of course speaking for the purposes of this question throughout the war - you have always been part of the political wing of the KLA as distinct from the military wing. Have I understood your evidence correctly, Mr. Krasniqi, about that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You know, sir, I do not mean the question rudely, but does it mean that literally you did not bear arms at all throughout the war but you performed other very important functions? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly I was a spokesperson for the KLA and I was a person in charge for meetings with the Western politicians and diplomats who used to come and meet and to discuss with the KLA representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again I want to be clear. Does it follow from that that you did not and did not participate in any actual fighting? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in fighting; I declared that earlier. I was not a soldier; I was a political representative to convey to the media, to the public, the voice of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And so that we understand the general principles that you applied to that job, as I think you indicated to us last Thursday, you saw your job as representing and publicising the policy of the General Staff of the KLA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Does it follow from your answers over the last few moments that you were alone in performing this job as spokesperson or did you have any assistants, colleagues, to help you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosova I was alone. I was the only one responsible for presenting -- publicising the policy of the KLA to the West and Germany, Switzerland, and other European countries. For these countries it was Bardhyl Mahmuti.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That means, then, does it, sir, that you are the writer, the author, of the various communiques that we have seen? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, because the communiques usually were about the operational -- operations in the zones. I was responsible for the political statements and such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Where we have seen, for example, a mixture of content in some of those communiques which I think could fairly be separated out between as operational and political, you would be responsible for the political input, others for the military. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look, please, at the three documents that we had translated over the -- Mr. Whiting had translated. I can't claim credit for something I haven't done - over the weekend for which we are grateful. Can you have in front of you P141, P142, and P143, and you'll need these in the Albanian of course. P141 first of all is the text of a speech that you gave. You've given us detailed evidence to the circumstances on the 3rd or 4th of March of 1998. Have you got that one there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Again, I don't know if it's the same on the Albanian, but I'm looking at the second page of the English and I'm looking at a paragraph that begins: "We are fully confident that in none of the mentioned valid documents can the defending of one's national threshold and dignity be assessed as a terrorist act." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What you're referring to there, Mr. Krasniqi, it seems, are things that are dealt with in the preceding paragraph, United Nations Charters and the like stretching from the Atlantic through Helsinki down to Paris. I want to ask you about the second sentence of that next paragraph: "Not a single liberation war in any country of the world has been qualified as a terrorist one, and our war is nothing but a liberation one." Are they your words, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. The entire text is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it right that not a single liberation war in any country of the world has been called a terrorist one? May I give you two examples: the Kenyan uprising in the 1950s and the formation of the state of Israel in 1948. Weren't they terrorist wars?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know them as being terrorist wars. It depends who has said this and what were the underlying motives of those who have described liberation wars as terrorist wars. Of course those who are occupiers find it difficult to call a liberation war otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you not know that Menachem Begin, before he became prime minister of Israel, was convicted of terrorist offences in the 1940s war of liberation the Israelis fought against the English? Did you not know that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you go, please, to P142, the Political Statement Number 2 of April 1998 and I want to ask you about something Mr. Whiting asked you about. Again, was this communique written in its entirety by you?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This communique -- the largest part of it has been written by me, but we have cooperated or there have been other people who have written about the political situation, people who have been outside of Kosova. The text was written by me. It was -- that part that was written by others. The text was sent to comrades outside of Kosova; they revised it and sent it back to us. In fact, it was a production of the KLA General Staff I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Krasniqi, were any of the comrades to whom this document was shown in draft form or any of the comrades who contributed to this document lawyers, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may -- it was possible at that time to consult lawyers, people who were versed in political issues and -- as well as the military ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sure it was possible and I can assure you, sir, I hope I have good reason for asking you specific questions. Before this document was circulated, this communique, as far as you can recollect were lawyers consulted either within or outside Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And were these lawyers familiar with international treaties and the like as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Who wrote the line, the second sentence of the document: "The KLA recognises and respects the international treaties of the United Nations and the Conventions on war"? Did you write that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I have written it even though a long time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we recognise that and I know the Tribunal will take that very much into account and I also recognise that textual analysis is difficult after all this time. But you see, these are words I suspect that we're going to hear much more as this case unfolds after you leave us, Mr. Krasniqi. I want to focus on "The KLA recognises and respects the international treaties of the United Nations and the Conventions on war." Had you read the international treaties of the UN and Conventions on war before the 29th of April, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a historian by profession. I possess sufficient information on international documents which have been issued earlier, especially after the Second World War. I'm talking about historical aspect of such documents because I'm not a lawyer myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The phrase "international treaties of the United Nations" has for lawyers and I'm sure historians a precise meaning, Mr. Krasniqi. My question, sir, is this: Had you read or received legal advice about the international treaties of the UN with regards to war before issuing this communique?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm repeating it. I didn't look at such issues from the point of view of a lawyer and I never broke down each and every word of such sentences. I looked at them from the historian and politician's point of view and not that of a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you understand what is meant in lawyers' language as armed conflict, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A war is an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you understand or don't you armed conflict to have a special particular and important meaning for this Tribunal? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the Tribunal, but in the political -- Oxford Political Dictionary, it is said that war is an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I deserved that. I didn't know the library here ran to the Oxford dictionary. Let's look over the page to page 6, shall we please, Mr. Krasniqi. And it really follows on from what we've just been talking about. And please forgive me for a close textual analysis. This is important, I assure you. Under the heading "The Homeland is Calling!", paragraph 6 begins with the exclamation: "We are in a state of war!" Did you write that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter who wrote it. I said that the document is issued by the General Staff. I may have written something. I have claimed paternity to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, if you would be good enough, Mr. Krasniqi, to bear with me. I think I shall decide what matters or not for the purposes of my questions, so if you would be good to answer it. Did you write the words "we are in a state or war," or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have written such sentences often; this might be one of them. It was a wartime for us -- actually, it was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I was going to make a suggestion and it's this: Should this Tribunal read that declaration as being from you as father of it, simply a statement of the reality of the situation, that you were indeed in a state of war as of April 1998 fighting the Serbs? Is that what you were seeking to express or something more meaningful?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Political dictionaries say that the war is a continuation of politics with arms of -- firearms. And this is what was happening in Kosova. Politics was exhausted -- political means were exhausted and what was being used were the firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn to the last of the documents in that little bundle, P143, please, which I think is Political Statement Number 5. Mr. Krasniqi, we've moved on in time now. We're now 28th of July of 1998. And again, may we assume you are the author of this document or at least as you put it --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the General Staff. It's Statement Number 5. I may be the author of this statement or to say it in fewer words, I'm the author that has been approved and atoned by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if you could go to the last page, or rather the last paragraph. I'm looking for a sentence that begins "We appeal to the international community." Could you let us know when you've found that, please, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. "We appeal to the international community to seriously not declaratively warn Belgrade, to support the just liberation war, which is protected by all international conventions of peace and war, while at the same time condemning the fascist Belgrade regime, which only understands the language of force." Again, really, it's the same question that related to the first of these three. "Protected by all international conventions of peace and war," was that your understanding as a historian or your advice you received from lawyers in the KLA? Or was it just a piece of journalism?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not consult with lawyers of course, but it might be both political and historic, even journalistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask you on those documents. Thank you very much, Mr. Krasniqi, you can put those away now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps they can be taken from you so -- 141, 142, and 143, if you can -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'd like, please, to move on if I may to deal with the second area I wanted to ask you about, and that is collaborators. Can I begin with an attempt at a definition again, Mr. Krasniqi, as a working definition. A collaborator, I suggest, is one who cooperates traitorously with an enemy. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When you are speaking about of collaborators, and you mention it in a number of different contexts in your evidence last week and I'm going to ask you about some of them, I wonder if we should attempt to draw a distinction. May I suggest one for your consideration, please. A distinction between civilians, or the modern phrase "noncombatants," on the one hand and people who could be properly described as collaborators on the one. Mr. Krasniqi, is that a distinction you recognise?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise it, but I need to explain something here. I mentioned this last week as well. The word "collaborator" is not an Albanian word. It is a foreign word that has entered Albanian dictionaries and its origin is in the Second World War and onwards. As to how we use it, it is possible that we have used it maybe not properly because we didn't have time to deal -- to refine words, but with us the collaborators were mentioned in context of those who were recruited by the Serb Security Service and who served the violent apparatus in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. To cooperate traitorously with an enemy, contains, does it not, two distinct aspects: Cooperation and traitorously. It would not be a traitorous cooperation to be seen speaking to a Serb, would it, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It wouldn't necessarily be seen as a traitorous cooperation to sell bread to a Serb, would it, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I think I have explained this in the first part of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. Just answer my questions, if you would be good enough. It's not traitorous cooperation to sell wood to a Serb, is it, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not. And we never mixed those who were recruited by Serbian Secret Service with those civilians who lived in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the 10th of February when you were giving evidence here last week you attempted a definition in answer to Mr. Whiting's question of what a collaborator is. And at page 40, line 19 to be exact, you said that they were in the service of the violent Serb regime. And you went on to give us, you may recollect, Mr. Krasniqi, a memorable concrete example, as you described it, of the Dr. Hafir Shala. You remember telling us all this last week? I see you nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Once war had broken out - and I mean the word in the looser sense, Mr. Krasniqi - in April 1998 which lasted up to and included and a little later on including the bombing by NATO the following year, as far as ordinary law and order is concerned in your country, in Kosova, at that time, would I be right in suggesting, Mr. Krasniqi, that ordinary law and order had effectively been suspended during that period of the war?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosova, law and order did not exist since spring 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure there are many who would sit in that chair and disagree with that proposition, but nonetheless I'm not going to go all the way back to 1981. It was, was it not, in the autumn of 1998, I suggest, that the KLA formed the military police. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Part of their purpose it might be said, might it not, was to represent in part, I underline, a functioning police force as best as one could, given the war. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to see if I can understand the process that led to the execution of a collaborator, Mr. Krasniqi. First of all, given the answers to the questions you've just given us, it would follow, would it, that in the ordinary sense a police investigation, an arrest, an interrogation, a trial, a sentence was not what was happening. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: For a human life to be taken of a collaborator, is this Tribunal to assume that it was not something that was done lightly and for fun but seriously, for what was believed to be good purpose? What was the position, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to explain here the aim of our war was not to take human lives but to liberate Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I asked you whether the taking of a life of someone believed to be a collaborator was done lightly or seriously. What was the position, please?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not play with human lives. I will say it again. Our aim was not to take lives. Our aim was to liberate Kosova and we were in a war with the occupier, with Belgrade, and with the police and military forces of Belgrade as well as other forces who were serving this violent apparatus. And I don't see anything that I can add to this. Our purpose, our goal, was life, not death. Serbia was the one that was encouraging death everywhere in Kosova, in every village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In communique number 43 from the 4th of March of 1998, I want to draw your attention only to a ringing line to Mr. Whiting drew your attention to "Death to enemies and traitors!" Did you write that line?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not important who wrote that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Don't worry about what's important; the Court will decide that. Please answer my question: Did you write the line: "Death to enemies and traitors!"

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with it as a concept?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was and I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Does it in any sense in your mind, Mr. Krasniqi, detract or deflect from the very serious purpose of ending the life of someone believed to be a collaborator, a someone who cooperates traitorously with the enemy? Does such a line deflect from that purpose or not, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A legal principle says that law should not deal with minor things, and that's why I think that at times this Court is trying to evade the main purpose. I will repeat what I've already said several times during this evidence. Our war was directed against the Serb occupier, against the Serb police and military forces and the violent apparatus that served it. We shouldn't deal here with terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if I can attempt a conclusion to this aspect of these questions regarding collaborators, Mr. Krasniqi, trying to distil everything you've been saying to us over the last two days. As I understand your evidence it seems to come to this, see if you agree with me: That it was no part of KLA political or military policy to kidnap, torture, still less murder innocent civilians or noncombatants, call them what you will. Now, that's my attempt to distil your evidence. Would you agree with it or not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, we can't leave it there, Mr. Krasniqi, of course. We have to go on to the next step, and it's this: If, and I underline the word "if," this Tribunal were to come to the conclusion that such things happened it would follow, wouldn't it, that if that happened it could only have occurred at the hands of what I'll call rogue elements. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and I have said this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My phrase, not yours, but you've adopted it so I'll go on. Rogue elements, I suggest, that would have had to have been acting without the support, without the knowledge, or without the encouragement of anyone in authority or command. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, there's another component that we have to feed into all of this, Mr. Krasniqi, and I'd like you please for it to go to tab 8 of the file that Mr. Whiting provided you with. And this is an interview with Koha Ditore of the 2nd of September of 1998. And I think what you have with this is a newspaper article itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is there a larger version for Mr. Krasniqi? P144. Mr. Powles tells me it's P145. Thank you. Sorry, I didn't mean to trouble, Mr. Younis -- oh, Mr. Younis has a larger copy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm sorry to make you have to do this, but you're going to have to look for an answer of yours quite a way into this interview. It's the one that Mr. Whiting took you to: "We do not know anything about the imprisonment or kidnapping of any Serbian journalist or citizen."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's page 3 of 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you have that paragraph, Mr. Krasniqi: "We do not know anything of the kidnapping or imprisonment of any Serb citizens or journalists." This is your response?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. Can we just read that paragraph together, please. "The UCK has not taken up weapons to fight against Serbian journalists and citizens, but to fight against Serbian soldiers and terrorists that have reduced Kosova to ashes. After all the terror and devastation that have been seen in Kosova, it is impossible to keep under control the feelings of hatred and vengeance that the enemy himself has inspired. Despite our insistence that the Albanians' struggle must not resemble the barbarism practiced by the enemy." Mr. Krasniqi, as I say, this was, as it were, the next component on from the propositions that you and I were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given answer for this issue. Now I don't know, why should I give an answer to an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Because I'm about to ask -- because I'm about to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, it may have been but I want to ask you a different question to the one that was asked you before, so be patient with me, please. If -- if -- kidnapping, torture, murder occurred by the rogue elements I've talked about, then what cannot be discounted, can it, Mr. Krasniqi, is the possibility that that was occurring by individuals carrying out acts of revenge or vengeance to settle old scores. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Such things could have happened. I spoke of the Kosova Liberation Army, about its programme and its aims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You spoke of it as an army, as a force never taking revenge. Of course what you could not legislate for, could you, as a command structure was individual acts of barbarism. That you couldn't legislate for, could you? If they occurred.

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not support such acts even during the war and not today. And we will never support such acts. We would never even exercise such acts, acts that resembled the acts of the police and military -- Serb police and military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Just two more things I want to ask you about under the heading of collaborators before the rising of the court today, Mr. Krasniqi. The first is this: International support for the cause of the KLA was vital, was it not, from an early stage of the war and before it?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was and is still today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suppose one could say that the largest, perhaps, ever example of the obtaining of international support by a liberation movement was the NATO bombing that began in early 1999. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So it would appear therefore, wouldn't it, from those two propositions that the international community's support for the KLA and to avert a humanitarian disaster was sought and was obtained during 1998. And you played your part in that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you at any stage have any contact with the Kosovo Verification Mission for Human Rights, the OSCE, in late 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with a woman by the name of Susan Ringaard Pedersen who worked for that organisation?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a book produced by the OSCE entitled "As Seen, As Told" regarding the work of that organisation in Kosova during and after the war?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to read you a paragraph from a statement made by Susan Ringaard Pedersen from that organisation. It's a statement made to this Tribunal, paragraph 28 to be exact. And it might be a convenient moment at which to finish this evening, if Their Honours permit. What she says is this, Mr. Krasniqi: "Based on reports or complaints we received and information we gathered, the main reason for these abductions," and she's talking about abduction of civilians, "was collaboration with the enemy. I received information that the KLA kidnapped Kosovar Albanians and Romas only because they had a Serbian friend or were employed by a Serb. That seemed reason enough to be accused as a collaborator." And it goes on: "We also got the impression that the abductions or arrests committed by the KLA were systematic, preplanned, and organised. We had the impression that the KLA was really trying to pull the community apart." Now, Mr. Krasniqi, you've dealt with a good deal of that already. I wonder if you might be good enough to focus your response to that paragraph on the suggestion, the impression, that this was systematic, preplanned, and organised attempt to pull the community apart, that is to say the taking, torturing, and no doubt killing of innocent civilians. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that unfortunately this paragraph as it is is taken from a person who did not have good intentions about the citizens of Kosova and about the just war of the KLA. I know that there were such reports which said little about the main cause of the war and the situation in Kosova. I know that there have been attempts to blame the KLA as well, but myself, as its political representative, I am convinced that this was not the KLA policy and not even its aim. It wasn't its policy and aim to kidnap civilians and to call them collaborators, to call those people who had no other means to live but to get employed by Serbs or others. I'm convinced that not a single citizen of Kosova, regardless of whether he is Albanian or something else, did not become a victim of the KLA except for those who were recruited within the ranks of the Serb forces, military and police forces. Therefore, I cannot agree with a thing like that which to me is not true. The war was not incited by the KLA and its soldiers; the war came to Kosova as a consequence -- as a political consequence of Serbia, in order to exercise violence and genocide in Kosova. And this was supported by the well-known document of the Belgrade Academy of Science and Art. This was a systematic Serb policy which in several of its programmes aimed at making the Albanians of Kosova flee Kosova and making it impossible for the Albanians in Kosova to live --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JAKUP KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and forcing them to leave Kosova. And from 1981 to 1997, in these 10 or 15 years more than 400.000 Albanians, mainly youth, left Kosova and went to different European countries. And I know that each and every country of Europe knows how much these figures grew in France, in Switzerland, in Germany, throughout Europe, and in the United States. I know that both the European Union and the international community know that the Milosevic regime had a traditional policy to change the structure of Kosova and not its own citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to stop you and not least because it's 7.00 and about halfway through that we got several miles away from the question I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But that might be a convenient moment to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn for the night and continue tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
